pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 💻 **Strand 1 — Introduction To Computing**
Sub-strand 3: Health and Safety in the Use of ICT Tools

Using a computer for long hours with poor posture, loud earphones or unsafe cables can harm your body. In this unit you will learn about computer-related health problems, the rules that protect computer users, and how to set up and assess a safe and comfortable workstation.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B7.1.3.1** Demonstrate how to apply health and safety measures in using ICT tools.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B7.1.3.1.1** Describe health measures, current regulatory requirements and potential computing-related disorders.
- **B7.1.3.1.2** Describe safety measures in using ICT tools.
- **B7.1.3.1.3** Demonstrate how to apply health and safety measures in using ICT tools (including workstation health risk assessment methods).
- **B7.1.3.1.4** Explore safety measures at workstations.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 3.1 Computer-Related Health Problems and Regulations
- 3.2 Safety Measures in Using ICT Tools
- 3.3 Applying Health and Safety: Workstation Risk Assessment
- 3.4 Safety Measures at Workstations

**Core competencies developed:** Communication and Collaboration (CC8.1), Digital Literacy (DL5.1), Personal Development and Leadership (PL5.3), Critical Thinking and Problem Solving (CP5.7).

lessons.title: Computer-Related Health Problems and Regulations

pages.title: Computer-Related Health Problems and Regulations
Computer-Related Health Problems and Regulations (continued)
pages.body:
| **Disorder / hazard** | **Cause** | **Symptoms** | **Prevention** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Repetitive Strain Injury (RSI) | Repeating the same movements (typing, clicking, swiping) for long periods | Pain, stiffness, tingling in fingers, wrists, arms or shoulders | Take regular breaks; keep wrists straight; use ergonomic keyboards/mice; stretch |
| Carpal Tunnel Syndrome | Pressure on the median nerve in the wrist from bent wrists and constant typing | Numbness, tingling and weakness in the thumb and fingers, often worse at night | Keep wrists level; use a wrist rest; don’t rest wrists on sharp desk edges; take breaks |
| Computer Vision Syndrome (digital eye strain) | Staring at screens for long periods, glare, poor lighting, small text | Tired, dry or itchy eyes; blurred vision; headaches | Follow the **20-20-20 rule**; reduce glare; adjust brightness; enlarge text; blink often; see an optician |
| Hearing impairment | Loud earphones/headphones or standing near loud Public Address (PA) speakers | Ringing in the ears (tinnitus); gradual hearing loss | Keep volume below 60%, for no more than 60 minutes at a time; stand away from speakers |
| Back and neck pain | Poor posture, slouching, looking down at phones (“text neck”), badly placed screens | Aching back, neck and shoulders | Sit upright with back support; raise the screen to eye level; take breaks |
| Headaches and stress | Long hours, glare, noise, pressure to finish tasks | Headache, irritability, poor sleep | Plan work time; take breaks; avoid screens before bedtime |
| Inactivity-related problems | Sitting for hours without exercise | Weight gain, poor blood circulation | Stand up and move every hour; take part in sports |

pages.title: Computer-Related Health Problems and Regulations (continued)
pages.body:
> ✨ **Did you know? — The 20-20-20 rule** Every **20 minutes**, look at something about **20 feet (6 metres)** away for **20 seconds**. This relaxes the focusing muscles of your eyes.
## Current regulatory requirements
Many countries have laws and standards that require employers and schools to protect people who use computers. Important examples include:
- **Ghana Labour Act, 2003 (Act 651):** requires employers to provide safe and healthy working conditions, give workers necessary safety equipment and training, and report workplace accidents.
- **Factories, Offices and Shops Act, 1970 (Act 328), Ghana:** sets standards for cleanliness, lighting, ventilation, space and fire safety in offices and workplaces.
- **Display Screen Equipment (DSE) regulations** (used in the United Kingdom and widely adopted as good practice): employers must assess workstations, plan breaks, and provide eye tests and training for regular computer users.
- **International standards** such as **ISO 9241** describe ergonomic requirements for screens, keyboards and workstations.
- **WHO safe listening guidance:** limit exposure to loud sound and keep personal audio devices at safe volumes.
> 🧪 **Activity — Hazard spotting**
Watch a video or study pictures of bad body postures and other hazards in using computing devices. For each picture, identify the health hazard, the device involved, and one preventive measure. Present your answers in a table.

pages.title: Safety Measures in Using ICT Tools
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.3.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- describe safety measures when using ICT tools;
- explain the dangers of liquids, trailing cables and exposed electrical terminals.
| **Hazard** | **Danger** | **Safety measure** |
|---|---|---|
| Spilling liquids on computers | Water conducts electricity and can cause short circuits, electric shock, fire and permanent damage to circuit boards and keyboards. | No food or drinks in the computer lab. If a spill occurs: switch off and unplug immediately, tell the teacher, turn the device upside down and let it dry completely before use. |
| Trailing power and network cables | People can trip and fall; devices can be pulled off desks; cables get damaged. | Route cables along walls or under desks; use cable covers or ties; never run cables across walkways. |
| Touching exposed live (positive) and neutral (negative) terminals | Electric shock, burns or death. | Never touch bare wires or open sockets; report damaged plugs and cables; don’t insert objects into sockets; only qualified electricians repair electrical faults. |
| Overloaded sockets | Overheating and fire. | Use one plug per socket or a fused multi-socket extension; don’t chain extensions together. |
| Poor ventilation / blocked vents | Overheating of equipment; fire risk. | Keep vents clear; don’t use laptops on beds or cushions. |
| Fire | Injury, loss of equipment and data. | Keep a **CO₂ fire extinguisher** for electrical fires (never use water); know the fire exits; switch off power at the mains if safe. |

pages.title: Safety Measures in Using ICT Tools (continued)
pages.body:
> 🛡️ **Safety first — Laboratory rules**
1. Enter the lab only with permission.
2. No food, drinks or water bottles near computers.
3. Do not touch cables, plugs or sockets with wet hands.
4. Report any damaged equipment, sparks or burning smell immediately.
5. Shut down computers properly at the end of the lesson.
6. Keep bags out of walkways.

pages.title: Applying Health and Safety: Workstation Risk Assessment
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.3.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain what a workstation health risk assessment is;
- explore risks associated with workstations and how to overcome them;
- carry out a simple workstation risk assessment.
A **workstation** is the area where a person uses a computer: the desk, chair, computer, screen, keyboard, mouse, lighting and the space around them. A **workstation health risk assessment** is a careful check to find anything that could harm the user, decide how likely and serious the harm is, and decide what to do to remove or reduce it.
## Steps in a risk assessment
1. **Identify the hazards**: look at the chair, desk, screen, lighting, cables and electrical connections.
2. **Decide who might be harmed and how**: learners, teachers, cleaners.
3. **Evaluate the risk**: how likely is the harm and how serious would it be? (low, medium or high)
4. **Take action**: remove the hazard or reduce the risk.
5. **Record and review**: write down the findings and check again regularly.
| **Risk at the workstation** | **How to overcome it** |
|---|---|
| Wrist pains | Keyboard and mouse close together at elbow height; wrists straight; use a wrist rest; take short breaks |
| Eye problems | Screen at arm’s length; reduce glare from windows; adjust brightness and text size; 20-20-20 rule |
| Back and neck pains | Adjustable chair with back support; top of screen at eye level; feet flat on floor |
| Faulty electrical connections | Inspect plugs and cables; replace damaged ones; use a qualified electrician; do not overload sockets |

pages.title: Applying Health and Safety: Workstation Risk Assessment (continued)
pages.body:
> 💻 **Practical session — Workstation risk assessment checklist**
Work in pairs. Use the checklist below to assess one workstation in your lab. Tick **Yes** or **No**, and suggest an action for every **No**.
| **Check** | **Yes** | **No** | **Action needed** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chair height adjusted so feet rest flat on the floor |  |  |  |
| Back is supported by the chair |  |  |  |
| Top of screen at or slightly below eye level |  |  |  |
| Screen about an arm’s length away |  |  |  |
| No glare or reflections on the screen |  |  |  |
| Keyboard and mouse within easy reach; wrists straight |  |  |  |
| Cables tidy and not across walkways |  |  |  |
| Plugs, sockets and cables undamaged; sockets not overloaded |  |  |  |
| Enough space and ventilation around the equipment |  |  |  |
| No food or drink at the workstation |  |  |  |

pages.title: Safety Measures at Workstations
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.3.1.4
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- identify measures that eliminate workstation hazards;
- explain how to minimise risks that cannot be eliminated.
[[fig:c7-f11|Figure 10: Correct posture at a computer workstation]]
**Ergonomics** is the study of designing equipment and work areas so that they fit the human body, preventing discomfort and injury. The best approach is to **eliminate** a hazard completely; where that is not possible, **minimise** (reduce) the risk.
| **Measure** | **Eliminate or minimise?** | **How** |
|---|---|---|
| Evaluating the display screen | Minimise | Check the screen is clean, stable (no flicker), and that brightness and contrast are comfortable. Tilt it to avoid reflections. Use Night light/blue-light settings in the evening. |
| Adjusting the chair for comfort | Minimise | Raise or lower the seat so elbows are about 90° and thighs level; adjust the backrest to support the lower back; use a footrest if feet do not reach the floor. |
| Avoiding potential slips and falls | Eliminate | Keep floors dry and free of bags; tie up cables; ensure good lighting; clean spills at once. |
| Re-positioning devices | Minimise | Place the screen directly in front; keep keyboard and mouse at the same height and close; place printers so users don’t twist; use a document holder. |
| Removing faulty equipment | Eliminate | Label and remove damaged cables, plugs or machines until repaired. |
| Scheduling breaks | Minimise | Plan short breaks (5–10 minutes every hour) to stretch and rest the eyes. |

pages.title: Safety Measures at Workstations (continued)
pages.body: > 💡 **Summary Remember** Good posture: **back supported, shoulders relaxed, elbows at 90°, wrists straight, screen at eye level, feet flat**. Good habits: **take breaks, blink, stretch, keep volume safe, keep liquids away**.

pages.body:
> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.
## Short answer questions
1. Name **four** computer-related health disorders, their causes and prevention.
2. Explain **three** safety measures relating to electricity in the computer lab.
3. What is a workstation health risk assessment? Outline its steps.
4. Distinguish between eliminating and minimising a workstation hazard, with an example of each.
## Practical tasks
1. Adjust your chair, screen and keyboard to the correct posture shown in Lesson 3.4 and demonstrate it to your teacher.
2. Complete the workstation checklist for three computers in your lab and present a summary of the actions needed.
